Rules summary Contents 1 Aim 2 Turn Sequence 3 Stage 1: Gain 4 Stage 2: Combat 4.1 Matching Symbols 4.2 Attack 4.3 Heal 4.4 Steal 4.5 Defend 4.6 Spell Sets / Rituals 4.7 Creatures 4.8 Auras 4.9 Curses 5 End Turn 6 End Game 7 Dice Sides 7.1 Blue Dice (12) 7.2 Red Dice (8) 8 Strategy Tips Aim Deplete your enemy's health to eliminate them and win the battle. Turn Sequence Each turn is split into 2 stages: Gain and Combat. Stage 1: Gain In the Gain stage gather the dice earned by your creatures. Each creature in a player's army has a gain section. This determines the dice earned. The dice are then rolled. The wildcard symbol can be used in place of any other dice symbol. Stage 2: Combat In the Combat stage, players can use the actions available on their cards in any order. The player cannot use the same card action twice during the same turn. For the first turn, players may only cast and defend. Matching Symbols When using an action, the player must match all symbols needed for that action with symbols on the player's rolled dice. Those dice are then discared to activate the action. Some actions require creatures to be discarded. Any defense tokens associated with a discarded creature are removed. Once a player acquires a card, it can be used immediately if the player has the available symbols on the player's rolled dice. Attack Attack does damage to your opponent. If your opponent has active defense tokens, they may discard tokens equivalent to the damage. Otherwise the attack decreases your opponent's health. The defending player chooses which tokens are discarded. If your attack removes all your opponent's defense tokens, any damage left over decreases their health. Heal Heal increases the player's health. The player cannot heal over the maximum health of 30. Steal Steal does damage to your opponent like Attack and can increase your health. You gain health equal to the health lost by your opponent. Defense tokens prevent this. Defend Defend adds defense tokens to the chosen ability. These active defense tokens are used to defend against an opponent's attack. The player cannot activate a creature's defense if there are already active defense tokens on it. Spell Sets / Rituals Each player may only have a maximum of 6 spell sets and rituals. If the player learns a spell set or ritual over the maximum of 6, they can sacrifice one of their existing spell sets or rituals. Creatures Each player may only have a maximum of 6 creatures. If the player summons a creature over the maximum of 6, they can sacrfice one of their existing creatures. Auras Each player may only have a maximum of 1 aura. The casting of a new aura replaces the player's existing aura. Curses Each player may only have a maximum of 1 curse. The casting of a new curse replaces the opponent's existing curse. When casting a curse, it is placed on your opponent's player area. Curses last 3 turns and are then discarded. End Turn The player may end their turn at any moment during the Combat stage. A maximum of 2 blue dice and 2 red dice can be kept. All other dice are discarded. The kept dice are rerolled on the player's next Gain stage along with any other dice they gain. Play continues to the next player. End Game The game ends when one player's health goes to 0. That player is eliminated. The remaining player wins and is declared the greatest summoner in the land. Dice Sides Blue Dice (12) 3 Mercury, 2 Salt, 1 Wildcard Red Dice (8) 2 Salt, 2 Sulphur, 2 Wildcard Strategy Tips Strategy Tips

[Rating: 1/10] It seems the game favours a long game strategy and once you reach that point the game is already decided by the monster and spell configuration but it just keeps on going and going, the dice are cute but the art is not really appealing.

[Rating: 1/10] Seems so dated, there can be much better games out there. Uninteresting after a while.

[Rating: 2/10] I hate these types of 2 player, push and pull type games where do you focus on defense, do you just focus on attack, or focus on getting a bunch of dice?  For me there is very little going on besides roll and do some actions, which makes it very boring.  Add in art that just does not look good, and it's a hard pass for me.

[Rating: 2/10] Fun, 2 turns no salt and your done. Not much dept or different strategies possible.

[Rating: 3/10] At least in its basic mode (i.e. with the suggested starting cards) this has not nearly enough variation in effects or tactics to make it interesting. There's a power curve, you want to go just enough farther along it than your opponent to crush them before they build their tableau.

[Rating: 3/10] Dice games always call to me, but Dice Summoners is lacking in several areas. The core loop is to accumulate dice quickly and then pivot to damage maximization, and there aren't sufficient mechanisms to create exciting counters. The game ends up feeling like a slow race rather than an epic battle of mages.

[Rating: 3/10] Very limited choices. Just spend dice on the same actions every turn and see who dies first. Most rounds boil down to whoever can pile up the biggest amount of dice first, which basically means buying creatures and advanced creatures, until your bank is full. From that point on, you try to do all the damage you can while maintaining just the right amount of defense to not die next round. This process alone took like 40 minutes for us, was very mathy and very boring.

[Rating: 4/10] After players gain 6 advanced cfeatures (and some mystical) the game transform into pure dice fest without decisions. So all decisions (may be) could be taken in the deck building phase. That pendulum can take a long time in the end of the game.

[Rating: 4/10] Interesting combat game that suffers from a runaway leader problem and some really poor graphic design.

[Rating: 4/10] The game didn't feel well balanced. Getting creatures out gets you more dice to do more in the future. The ritual creatures never seemed worth it. The curses and auras didn't seem worth it unless you got them early on. Spells were worth it since they do more damage / defense.  It was just a matter of focusing on summoning creatures and learning spells until switching to attacking with every die and overwhelming the opponents defense. Our games were more like 15 minutes. And I didn't care for the artwork either.

[Rating: 4/10] 1v1 dice-based "Combative" engine builder - except one of the early important pieces is 'more dice', and faces are all similar enough that you pretty much always go for that first, then throw attacks/defenses until someone crumbles. Not a lot of room for variation outside of luck, since there aren't really many strategies to go around.

[Rating: 4/10] I've only played this once with the beginner setup, but unless the other setups have interesting combos this game felt really boring.
